title: The Estate, the Fortress, and the Way Around the World: Bakunin from Pryamukhino to the Bremgarten Ground
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Pryamukhino, birth on the family estate
stops.date_confidence: attested; 30 May 1814 New Style, 18 May Old Style, per en. and ru.wikipedia
stops.campa: On the family estate at Pryamukhino in Tver province, in a house of eleven children, a third child and oldest son is born to Alexander Bakunin, a landowner retired from the diplomatic service in Italy who plants an English garden and teaches his daughters Rousseau. The shelves hold German philosophy and the fields hold serfs. Mikhail grows up among his sisters in a household where argument is the family sport and where the estate church, begun in 1808, will not be consecrated until he is twenty-two. Sixty-two years later he is buried in Bern. No museum is ever made of the house.
suggested_refs: The Pryamukhino estate church, begun 1808 to a probable design by N. A. Lvov, consecrated October 1836

stops.name: St Petersburg, the Artillery School on the Arsenal embankment
stops.date_confidence: attested by ru.wikipedia as 1829; the first research pass gave 1828, and the disagreement is left standing
stops.campa: He is sent at fifteen to the Mikhailovsky Artillery School at Arsenalnaya 17, on the Vyborg side of the Neva, and is commissioned an officer in January 1833. He hates the drill, the barracks, and the mathematics of gunnery, which he can do and does not want to do. In June 1834 the school expels him for insolence to its commandant, General Sukhozanet, and posts him west to an artillery brigade on the Polish frontier. His father had intended a career. The army returns to the family a young man who has learned one thing: he cannot be commanded.
suggested_refs: The Mikhailovskoye Artillery School buildings on Arsenalnaya naberezhnaya, founded 1820, distinct from the engineering school in Mikhailovsky Castle

stops.name: The Minsk frontier, the posting abandoned
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the exact garrison is disputed among biographers and the month is not documented
stops.campa: Posted to the marshy country between Minsk and Grodno, in a province still being punished for the rising of 1830, Bakunin serves a season and then stops serving. He leaves the brigade without permission and goes home to Pryamukhino; by the end of 1835 the discharge is formal, and he is a gentleman of twenty-one with no profession, no income, and a father who has stopped speaking to him about the future. Biographers dispute which garrison it was and what he saw of the frontier. He never holds a salaried post again in his life.
suggested_refs: E. H. Carr's account of the Belarusian posting, the only sustained treatment reachable

segments.name: Moscow, Berlin, and the Creative Passion

stops.name: Moscow, the Stankevich circle
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; en. and ru.wikipedia both put the move at 1835, correcting the 1840 given in one research array
stops.campa: Discharged and in disgrace, he moves to Moscow and tries to keep himself by teaching mathematics, which fails. He falls instead into the circle of Nikolai Stankevich, where young Russians read Fichte and then Hegel, in German, at night, as if philosophy were contraband, which under Nicholas I it half is. Here he acquires the vocabulary he never puts down: negation, dialectic, freedom won through struggle. Vissarion Belinsky quarrels with him; Ivan Turgenev will put a version of him in a novel. Five years pass in these rooms and he publishes nothing.
suggested_refs: The Stankevich circle of Moscow, 1831-1839, and its manuscript translations of Hegel

stops.name: Berlin, the university on Unter den Linden
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1840; the month of enrolment is not documented in reachable sources
stops.campa: Money borrowed from Alexander Herzen carries him to Berlin, where he enrols at the university and takes his seat in the lecture halls on Unter den Linden. He arrives nine years after Hegel died in the chair the place is still arguing about, and he drifts left into the Young Hegelians, the milieu that is at the same moment producing Marx and Engels. He never takes a degree. Philosophy stops being a destination here and becomes a staging ground. He is twenty-six years old and his family in Tver still expects a professor.
suggested_refs: The Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universitat lecture halls on Unter den Linden, and the chair Hegel held until 1831

stops.name: Berlin, Schelling at the rostrum
stops.date_confidence: attested; three corpus journeys independently record the same dated lecture and name Bakunin in the audience
stops.campa: The Prussian state summons the old Schelling from Munich to kill Hegelianism in its own house, and on the fifteenth of November the hall cannot hold the people who come. Bakunin sits in the crush. So does Soren Kierkegaard, so does Friedrich Engels, so does Jacob Burckhardt, and Alexander von Humboldt, seventy-two years old, is in the room. Three separate journeys of this atlas record the same afternoon from three separate seats. Bakunin leaves unconvinced. He takes from the afternoon what he takes from every lecture: the negation interests him and the system does not.
suggested_refs: Schelling's inaugural Berlin lecture, 15 November 1841, and the surviving auditors' notes

stops.name: Dresden, the passion for destruction
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of publication in the Deutsche Jahrbucher; the month is conventional
stops.campa: He leaves Berlin for Dresden and for Arnold Ruge's Deutsche Jahrbucher, and publishes there, over the invented French name Jules Elysard, the essay that ends in the sentence anarchists will be quoting a century and a half later. On its face it is still an argument about Hegel. In substance it is already an instruction. Russian agents read German journals as a matter of routine, and the pseudonym holds for a while and then does not. Within the year the ministry in St Petersburg orders him home, and he declines to go home.
stops.quote: Let us therefore trust the eternal Spirit which destroys and annihilates only because it is the unfathomable and eternally creative source of all life. The passion for destruction is a creative passion, too.
stops.quote_source: Die Reaktion in Deutschland, Deutsche Jahrbucher, 1842, published as Jules Elysard; English translation on marxists.org
suggested_refs: Deutsche Jahrbucher, 1842, the Jules Elysard essay

stops.name: Zurich, the order to come home
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month of arrival is not documented
stops.campa: With the Russian secret police now interested in him, Bakunin crosses into Switzerland and settles in Zurich, where he meets Wilhelm Weitling, a communist tailor who preaches a coming revolution in the language of the gospels and who is arrested with Bakunin's name among his papers. The order arrives from St Petersburg to return at once. He refuses it. In 1844 the Senate strips him in absentia of noble rank and property rights and rules that Siberia awaits him if he is ever taken. He is thirty and has become, on paper, nobody.
suggested_refs: The 1844 Senate decree stripping Bakunin of rank and property in absentia

stops.name: Paris, the two rivals and the long nights
stops.date_confidence: attested for the residence 1844-1847; one research array gives the itinerant range as 1843-1847, and the difference is not adjudicated
stops.campa: He settles in Paris on the pin that half this atlas shares, in the years when the city holds every exile Europe has manufactured. He argues Hegel with Karl Marx until three in the morning and property with Pierre-Joseph Proudhon until later than that. Gustave Flaubert is finishing his hated law studies in the same quarter. Marx and Bakunin take each other's measure at once and distrust what they measure, respectfully; the fracture that will break the First International twenty-five years from now is already legible in these rooms, in German, over wine.
suggested_refs: The Paris emigre milieu of 1844-1847: Proudhon, Marx, Herwegh, the Polish democratic societies

stops.name: Paris, the Palais Royal in February
stops.date_confidence: attested for the February Revolution; his day-by-day movements within it are not documented
stops.campa: The barricades go up in February, Louis-Philippe abdicates, and Bakunin, who has spent thirteen years reading about revolution, walks into one. He throws himself into the street agitation and afterwards remembers the weeks as intoxication. Then he goes east, toward Prussian Poland, to join a rising that has collapsed before his coach reaches the frontier. The pattern holds for the next twenty-six years. He is always travelling toward an insurrection, and the insurrection is reliably a week ahead of him or a week behind.
suggested_refs: The February Revolution of 1848 in Paris and the Polish democratic committees that formed in its first weeks

segments.name: The Year of Revolutions and the Fortresses

stops.name: Prague, the Slav Congress on the island
stops.date_confidence: attested; the congress ran 2-12 June 1848 at Zofin Palace, correcting the Bethlehem Chapel location given in the first research pass
stops.campa: The congress opens in the Zofin Palace on the Vltava island, delegates from every Slav people held under Habsburg or Ottoman or Russian rule, arguing federation in three languages at once. Bakunin is the only Russian in the hall and the only delegate who wants the Tsar destroyed rather than petitioned. On the eleventh day Austrian artillery on the heights opens on the city, the congress dissolves into street fighting, and Bakunin fights. He writes the Appeal to the Slavs afterwards. In 1925 the island is renamed Slovansky ostrov after these eleven days in June.
suggested_refs: Zofin Palace on Slovansky ostrov, Prague, seat of the 1848 Slavic Congress

stops.name: Dresden, the barricades at the Kreuzkirche
stops.date_confidence: attested; the rising is crushed on 9 May 1849 and the co-presence is recorded in the corpus and in Wagner's memoirs
stops.campa: He is in Dresden in May, sleeping under the roof of the Royal Saxon Kapellmeister, and when the king runs and the barricades go up Bakunin advises the provisional government on where to build them. Richard Wagner climbs the tower of the Kreuzkirche and sends down reports of Prussian troop movements while Bakunin holds the streets underneath. The rising breaks on the ninth. Wagner escapes toward Weimar, a hiding place at Magdala, a false passport, and Switzerland; Bakunin is taken days later at Chemnitz. One afternoon forks into an opera cycle and a Siberian sentence.
suggested_refs: The Kreuzkirche tower, Wagner's observation post during the May 1849 rising
sources: Wagner's memoirs on the Dresden uprising

stops.name: Konigstein, the first death sentence
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the fortress name comes from Carr rather than from a document, and the month of transfer is not established
stops.campa: They hold him in the fortress of Konigstein on its rock above the Elbe, which the Saxons have never lost to anyone, and a Saxon court sentences him to death. The sentence is commuted, and Saxony, which does not want the responsibility of the most famous prisoner in Germany, hands him to Austria instead. Two governments have now decided that killing him would cost more than keeping him alive. A third will shortly decide the same thing. He has been in custody eight months and will not stand outside a wall again for twelve years.
suggested_refs: Konigstein Fortress above the Elbe, Saxon state prison
sources: E. H. Carr, Michael Bakunin (1937) (fortress name)

stops.name: Olmutz, chained to the wall
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the chaining is traditional and repeated across the biographies without a primary document reached this pass
stops.campa: Austria tries him at Olmutz in Moravia, sentences him to death a second time, and reprieves him a second time. For part of the confinement, the tradition holds, he is chained by the wrists to the wall of the cell. In May 1851 the Austrians deliver him at the Russian frontier to gendarmes who have been waiting there for him, and he crosses into the empire he has not seen for eleven years, in irons, under a sentence of Siberian exile passed in his absence seven years before by a Senate that had never met him.
suggested_refs: The Olmutz citadel prison and the 1851 handover at the Russian frontier

stops.name: St Petersburg, the Alekseevsky Ravelin and the Confession
stops.date_confidence: attested for the imprisonment 1851-1854; the Confession is written in 1851 at the direction of Nicholas I
stops.campa: They put him in the Alekseevsky Ravelin of the Peter and Paul Fortress, the cell kept for the empire's most dangerous men, and Nicholas I, curious about his prisoner, asks him to write. Bakunin writes over a hundred pages addressed to the Tsar in the voice of a repentant son, confessing everything about himself and naming nobody else. Scholars have been arguing about it since it surfaced. He calls his own revolution terrible and unprecedented, and he asks pardon. He keeps his comrades out of the document. It goes into the police archive and stays there seventy years.
stops.quote: The revolution I planned was terrible and unprecedented, although directed more against things than against people.
stops.quote_source: Confession to Tsar Nicholas I, 1851, translated by Robert C. Howes, excerpted on marxists.org
suggested_refs: The Alekseevsky Ravelin, Peter and Paul Fortress; the manuscript Confession in the Third Section archive

stops.name: Shlisselburg, the scurvy years
stops.date_confidence: attested for the years 1854-1857; the month of transfer is not documented
stops.campa: Alexander II succeeds his father and, working down the list of state prisoners, marks Bakunin for transfer rather than release. Shlisselburg stands on an island where the Neva leaves Lake Ladoga, water on every side and a long winter. Scurvy takes most of his teeth. His mother petitions the new Tsar in person, and in 1857, after three years here and three in the Ravelin, the sentence becomes what the Senate ordered back in 1844: exile in Siberia, for life, with his civil rights extinguished and no prospect of return.
suggested_refs: Shlisselburg Fortress on Lake Ladoga, and the 1857 petition of Varvara Bakunina to Alexander II

segments.name: Siberia and the Way Around the World

stops.name: Tomsk, exile and the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested for the exile beginning 1857 and the marriage in 1858; one research array wrongly dated the marriage to 1857
stops.campa: Tomsk is exile and not prison, and after six years of stone he is allowed a room, a street, and a wage as a merchant's clerk. He gives French lessons to the daughters of a Polish exile family and in 1858 marries one of them, Antonina Kwiatkowska, who is eighteen to his forty-four. Most accounts hold that the marriage was never a marriage in the ordinary sense. He is nevertheless a private man with an address for the first time since Dresden. A street in Tomsk still carries his name, and the wooden house it runs beside was later rebuilt in stone.
suggested_refs: Bakunin Street, Tomsk, and the rebuilt house of the exile years

stops.name: Irkutsk, the governor-general's relative
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Irkutsk residence and the kinship with Muravyov-Amursky are reported across the biographies without a document reached this pass
stops.campa: Nikolai Muravyov-Amursky, governor-general of Eastern Siberia and a distant cousin, brings the exile down to Irkutsk and gives him clerical work and a place at the dinner table. Bakunin repays the hospitality by reading the Amur frontier as a map. The governor-general has just annexed a thousand miles of river from China; the traffic on it is Russian, unsupervised, and staffed by officials who do what a letter from Irkutsk tells them to do. In 1861 Bakunin applies for a travel permit on commercial business, and is issued one.
suggested_refs: The 1858 Treaty of Aigun and the new Russian Amur, the administrative gap Bakunin walked through

stops.name: Nikolaevsk, the mouth of the Amur
stops.date_confidence: attested for the departure from Irkutsk on 5 June 1861 and arrival at the river mouth in July, correcting a June date in the first research pass
stops.campa: He leaves Irkutsk on the fifth of June with a permit that does not extend past the river mouth, takes the steamer Strelok down the Amur, and reaches Nikolaevsk in July. Here Siberia stops being a wall. He talks his way onto a vessel bound for De-Kastri, and at De-Kastri onto the American clipper Vickery, and the last Russian officer who could have stopped him accepts a story about a trading errand and lets him aboard. Behind him is a sentence for life. Ahead is the Sea of Okhotsk. He is forty-seven and has been held for twelve years.
suggested_refs: The steamer Strelok, the anchorage at De-Kastri, and the American clipper Vickery

stops.name: Hakodate, the treaty port
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the port call is well attested but the weeks he spent there are not documented in any source reached
stops.campa: The Vickery puts him ashore at Hakodate on the northern Japanese island, one of the harbours opened to foreigners two years earlier after two centuries of seclusion. Russian consular officials are in the town and none of them has been told to look for him. He is further from Europe than any Russian revolutionary has yet been, and for these weeks no government on earth knows where he is. He waits for southbound shipping among Ainu porters, whalers, and merchants selling coal and seaweed to the American fleet.
suggested_refs: Hakodate as a treaty port after 1859, and the Russian consulate established there

stops.name: Yokohama, passage across the Pacific
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Yokohama contacts vary between secondary accounts and Bakunin's own record of the weeks is thin
stops.campa: At Yokohama he finds the Western settlement on the mudflats of the bay, two years old and already a port. He secures passage on the SS Carrington, bound for San Francisco, and in the settlement's rooms he meets the Americans and, by some accounts, Joseph Heco, a shipwrecked Japanese fisherman who became a naturalised citizen of the United States and has come home as an interpreter. Bakunin writes almost nothing during these weeks. What he made of Japan, and what Japan made of him, is a gap in the record and stays one.
suggested_refs: The Yokohama foreign settlement of 1861 and the memoirs of Joseph Heco

stops.name: San Francisco, landfall
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Carrington arrives 15 October 1861 and Bakunin's letter from the city is dated that month
stops.campa: The Carrington makes San Francisco on the fifteenth of October and Bakunin walks down the gangway into a city eleven years old and full of men who arrived by improbable routes. He writes at once to Herzen and Ogarev in London to say that he is alive and to ask for money. Montgomery Street, where Eadweard Muybridge kept a bookshop until the year before his stagecoach went over in Texas, is two streets up from the wharf. The United States is six months into its civil war and nobody in the port takes any notice of the Russian.
stops.quote: I was able to escape Siberia and after having traveled for a long time on the Amour and through the coasts and straits of Tartarie, in crossing Japan, I have finally arrived in San Francisco.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Herzen and Ogareff, October 1861, translation on marxists.org
suggested_refs: Montgomery Street, San Francisco, in 1861

stops.name: Aspinwall, the isthmus by rail
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Panama route; the railroad crossing is the standard transit of the period and is not separately documented for him
stops.campa: Rather than round Cape Horn he crosses at the isthmus, on the Panama Railroad, forty-eight miles of track laid through fever swamp at a cost in Chinese and Irish lives that nobody counted properly. A passage that once took a sailing ship two months takes him a matter of hours. At Aspinwall, the Atlantic town the Colombians call Colon, he waits for the New York steamer. He is using the fastest transport link on earth, eight years old and built for gold, in order to get back to a revolution.
suggested_refs: The Panama Railroad, completed 1855, and the transit port of Aspinwall

stops.name: New York, received by the exiles
stops.date_confidence: attested for November-December 1861 in the United States; the day is not documented
stops.campa: He lands in New York and is passed around the emigre and abolitionist circles as a curiosity: the man who escaped Austrian chains, a Tsar's fortress, and Siberia, in that order. He goes on to Boston and meets veterans of 1848 and men of the anti-slavery movement, and leaves almost no trace of what he said to any of them. He is impatient. Herzen's press is in London and the Polish question is opening again. The American war does not hold him, and he takes ship for England in December.
suggested_refs: The German Forty-Eighter and abolitionist circles of New York and Boston in 1861

stops.name: London, the Free Russian Press
stops.date_confidence: attested for the end of December 1861; the day is given as the 27th in the standard accounts
stops.campa: At the end of December he reaches Herzen's household in London, sixteen years after the two men last saw each other and a full circuit of the globe since. Kolokol, the Bell, printed here by Herzen and Nikolai Ogarev, is at the height of its power inside Russia, smuggled over the frontier and read in the ministries. Bakunin starts at once pushing the paper toward insurrection, which Herzen does not want. Karl Marx is a few miles east in Soho, writing. The two will meet again in this city in 1864 and be civil for a while.
suggested_refs: Kolokol and the Free Russian Press in London, 1857-1867

segments.name: The Bell, the Baltic, and the Italian Cells

stops.name: Paris, the plate exposed by Nadar
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the photograph itself; tagged R in the research pass because only one source carries the date
stops.campa: He crosses to Paris in August and sits for Nadar. The plate is exposed on the seventh: a heavy man of forty-eight, the beard going grey, the eyes of somebody who has slept badly for twelve years, looking slightly off the lens. It becomes the face of anarchism, reproduced on pamphlets and banners and walls into the next century by people who know nothing of the Ravelin or the Amur. He is in the city for days only, and goes back to London and the Polish committees and the arguments with Herzen about the Bell.
suggested_refs: Nadar's portrait of Bakunin, Paris, 7 August 1862

stops.name: Stockholm, the Polish cause argued in Swedish halls
stops.date_confidence: attested; ru.wikipedia gives the arrival as 24 February 1863, correcting the June date in the first research pass
stops.campa: He arrives in Stockholm on the twenty-fourth of February, five weeks into the January Uprising in Russian Poland, to raise Scandinavian support for a landing on the Baltic coast. He speaks at public meetings and is feted by Swedish liberals. His argument is that the Polish cause is a Russian cause, and that no Russian is free while Poland is held. The Swedish government listens to its ambassador in St Petersburg instead. He stays in Sweden into the autumn, by which time the expedition he came for has already failed at sea.
suggested_refs: The Swedish public meetings of spring 1863 on the Polish question

stops.name: Malmo, the Ward Jackson detained
stops.date_confidence: attested that the ship left London in March and was detained at Malmo in spring; the exact day of detention is not established
stops.campa: The steamer Ward Jackson leaves London in March carrying arms and volunteers under the Polish general Teofil Lapinski, bound for the Lithuanian coast; Bakunin joins it en route rather than at any Swedish quay. The Swedes detain the ship at Malmo. The volunteers transfer to a smaller vessel, the surf off Kurland turns them back, and the expedition ends without a landing anywhere. Bakunin never in his life sets foot on Polish or Lithuanian soil, and the uprising he came to arm is finished by the following spring.
suggested_refs: The Lapinski expedition and the steamer Ward Jackson, 1863
sources: en.wikipedia, on the Lapinski naval expedition of 1863

stops.name: Florence, the International Brotherhood
stops.date_confidence: attested for Italian residence 1864-1867; Florence specifically and the Brotherhood's structure rest on Carr
stops.campa: He goes to Italy, settles in Florence, and begins the work that occupies the rest of his life, which is the founding of secret societies. The International Brotherhood is to be a body of sworn revolutionaries, graded, invisible, seeding cells across Europe from a centre that is him. Italy suits him: a country three years old, its unification half finished and widely resented, its radicals unemployed since Garibaldi. He writes constitutions for the Brotherhood in enormous detail and burns through the small remittances his family still sends from Tver.
suggested_refs: The statutes of the International Brotherhood, drafted in Italy from 1864

stops.name: Naples, the first real following
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Naples years 1865-1867 and the Friscia connection come from Carr rather than from documents reached this pass
stops.campa: In Naples he acquires his first real following: Saverio Friscia, a Sicilian doctor and freemason, and the young men who will become the Italian anarchist movement. He talks all night, borrows money he does not return, and writes thousands of pages he neither finishes nor publishes. Carlo Cafiero and Errico Malatesta come out of the milieu he seeds here. Sixteen years after he leaves the city, in a forge at Dovia di Predappio, a blacksmith called Alessandro Mussolini reads Bakunin aloud to his household and names his son for revolutionaries.
suggested_refs: The Neapolitan circle around Saverio Friscia, seedbed of Italian anarchism

stops.name: Geneva, the League of Peace and Freedom
stops.date_confidence: attested; the inaugural congress opened at 14:00 on 9 September 1867 at the Palais Electoral, not the Salle de la Reformation as the first pass had it
stops.campa: The League of Peace and Freedom holds its inaugural congress in Geneva on the ninth of September, with Garibaldi in the hall and John Stuart Mill and Victor Hugo lending their names to the committee. Bakunin joins it intending to capture it. He speaks to the effect that peace between states is impossible for as long as states exist, and that the League must therefore declare for the abolition of both together. The liberals decline. At the Bern congress the following September he walks out with fifteen signatures on a protest.
suggested_refs: The Palais Electoral, Geneva, and the League's 1867 inaugural congress

stops.name: Geneva, the Alliance of Socialist Democracy
stops.date_confidence: attested for the founding in autumn 1868; the day is not documented
stops.campa: Out of the walkout he builds the International Alliance of Socialist Democracy: atheist, collectivist, federalist, and equipped with a public organisation and a secret one behind it. The Alliance applies for admission to the International Working Men's Association, which Karl Marx founded at St Martin's Hall in London four years earlier and runs through its General Council. Marx reads the application as an attempt to plant a rival organisation inside his own, and he is not wrong. The Alliance dissolves as a body; its members enter one by one.
suggested_refs: The programme of the International Alliance of Socialist Democracy, Geneva 1868

stops.name: Minusio, the Villa Baronata
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Baronata years 1869-1874 rest on Carr, and Bakunin was resident only at intervals. Contradiction left standing: the purchase by Cafiero is dated 1873 in the reference note, which cannot be reconciled with a 1869 installation, and no document was reached to adjudicate
stops.campa: Carlo Cafiero, who has an inheritance, buys the Villa Baronata on the slope above Lake Maggiore near Locarno and installs Bakunin in it. The house is meant to be a refuge and a revolutionary headquarters and becomes a ruin of accounts: Bakunin builds, plants, digs, and orders improvements at Cafiero's expense until the friendship breaks over the ledgers. He is here at intervals from 1869 almost to the end. It is where he writes when he writes, and where the letters arrive from Spain, from the Jura watchmakers, and from Italy.
suggested_refs: The Villa Baronata at Minusio above Lake Maggiore, bought by Carlo Cafiero in 1873

stops.name: Locarno, the letter to Nechayev
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the letter of 2 June 1870 survives and is translated on marxists.org
stops.campa: Sergei Nechayev arrives in Switzerland the previous year claiming to represent a Russian revolutionary committee that does not exist, and Bakunin, fifty-five years old and hungry for a young executioner, signs certificates for him and lends him his name. Nechayev murders a student in Moscow, takes Bakunin's correspondence, and blackmails a publisher using it. On the second of June Bakunin writes him the letter of a man who has been used and knows it, and who is still, in the same paragraphs, explaining method to the person who used him.
stops.quote: You are playing with Jesuit methods as a child plays with a doll.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Sergey Nechayev, 2 June 1870, translation on marxists.org
suggested_refs: The 2 June 1870 letter to Nechayev; the disputed authorship of the Catechism of a Revolutionary
sources: Paul Avrich on the Nechayev affair (attribution contested)

stops.name: Lyon, the Hotel de Ville taken
stops.date_confidence: attested for the September 1870 Lyon rising; the details of the seizure and escape rest on Carr
stops.campa: The Empire falls at Sedan, the Prussians march on Paris, and Bakunin goes to Lyon, where a committee of local radicals seizes the Hotel de Ville on the twenty-eighth of September. He posts from the building a decree declaring the administrative and governmental machinery of the state abolished. The National Guard retakes the hall the same day. He is held briefly in a cellar, freed by workers who come for him, and leaves the city in disguise. It is the last insurrection he takes part in with his own body rather than his correspondence.
suggested_refs: The Lyon decree of 28 September 1870 abolishing the state

stops.name: Marseille, the last hiding place
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Marseille month comes from Carr and is not documented elsewhere in sources reached
stops.campa: He hides in a room in Marseille for a month while the police look for him, weighing whether the south can be raised where Lyon could not. He decides that it cannot, and sails for Genoa at the end of October under a name that is not his. The Paris Commune breaks out in March without him. He writes about it instead, and his account becomes the anarchist reading of the Commune: not a government but the refusal of one. He is fifty-six, ill, and finished as a man who climbs onto barricades.
suggested_refs: Bakunin's writings on the Paris Commune, 1871

stops.name: The Hague, the expulsion
stops.date_confidence: attested; the congress sits 2-7 September 1872 and is the only one Marx attends in person
stops.campa: The Fifth Congress of the International meets at The Hague in the first week of September, the only congress Karl Marx attends in person, and he comes to finish Bakunin. The Bakuninists are outvoted. Bakunin and James Guillaume are expelled on charges built partly out of the Nechayev business, and the General Council is moved to New York, where it dies quietly of distance. Bakunin is not in the hall. Two weeks later the anti-authoritarian federations meet at Saint-Imier in the Jura and declare the expulsion void.
stops.quote: Mr. Marx does not believe in God, but he believes deeply in himself.
stops.quote_source: On the International and Karl Marx, letter to La Liberte, 1872, translation on marxists.org
suggested_refs: The Hague Congress of 1872 and the Saint-Imier congress of the anti-authoritarian federations

stops.name: Locarno, Statism and Anarchy
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of writing and anonymous publication; the month is not established
stops.campa: He writes Statism and Anarchy in Russian, for Russians, and it is printed anonymously in Switzerland and smuggled east, where the young populists going to the people read it as an instruction manual. It carries his indictment of Marx's socialism: that a dictatorship of the proletariat means the dictatorship of the few former workers who cease to be workers the moment they govern, and that the state which abolishes classes will manufacture a new class of engineers and clerks who own it. Forty-four years later Russia tests the argument.
stops.quote: If there is a State, there must be domination of one class by another and, as a result, slavery; the State without slavery is unthinkable.
stops.quote_source: Statism and Anarchy, 1873, translation on marxists.org
suggested_refs: Gosudarstvennost i Anarkhiya, printed anonymously in Switzerland, 1873

stops.name: Bologna, the rising that does not start
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the insurrection was set for 7 August 1874
stops.campa: The Italians plan a rising for the seventh of August in Bologna, and Bakunin comes down from Switzerland to be present at it and, by his own account, to die on a barricade if there is one. The police arrest Andrea Costa days beforehand and the improvised plan comes apart; the armed bands who reach the outskirts find no city in revolt and scatter in the dark. Bakunin waits in a house with a pistol. When it is clear that nothing will happen he leaves the country in disguise, north, back to the Baronata. He is sixty.
suggested_refs: The Bologna insurrection of 7 August 1874, organised by Cafiero and Andrea Costa

stops.name: Bern, the workingmen's hospital
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; ru.wikipedia carries the death date and the reported words on arrival
stops.campa: He comes up from Lugano in June, in the care of friends, to a workingmen's hospital in Bern and the physician Adolf Vogt, and tells them on arrival why he has come. In the last week he refuses broth and takes only buckwheat porridge. He talks about the Slavs and about what is coming. He dies at midday on the first of July, sixty-two years old, without a country, a party, a functioning organisation, or money. The Alliance is dissolved, the International is dead in two pieces, and the movement that will carry his name has not been founded yet.
stops.quote: I came here either for doctors to restore me or to close my eyes forever.
stops.quote_source: Bakunin to friends on arriving in Bern from Lugano, June 1876, reported in ru.wikipedia from period accounts
suggested_refs: The Burgerspital of Bern and the physician Adolf Vogt

stops.name: Bern, the Bremgarten ground
stops.date_confidence: attested; plot 9201, grave 68, and the mourner count are confirmed verbatim by ru.wikipedia, and the coordinates by de.wikipedia
stops.campa: He is buried on the fourth of July in the Bremgarten cemetery inside the city of Bern, plot 9201, grave 68. Over two hundred mourners follow the coffin: Germans, Poles, Swiss, Russians, watchmakers down from the Jura, men who will be expelled from four countries in the coming decade. There are speeches in several languages and a quarrel about one of them. Friends pay for the headstone. No state, no party, and no international afterwards takes custody of the grave, and no source consulted records a public monument to him anywhere.
suggested_refs: Bremgartenfriedhof, Bern, plot 9201, grave 68

stops.name: Geneva, the unfinished book printed
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of publication; the month is not established
stops.campa: Six years after the funeral, Carlo Cafiero and Elisee Reclus go through the papers, find an unfinished manuscript from 1871, and print it as Dieu et l'Etat. It is a fragment. It breaks off in the middle of an argument. It becomes the most translated anarchist text in the world: into English by Benjamin Tucker, then into Spanish, Italian, Yiddish, Chinese, Japanese. The man who finished almost nothing he began is read, for the next hundred and forty years, chiefly in a book he did not finish and never saw bound.
stops.quote: I reverse the phrase of Voltaire, and say that, if God really existed, it would be necessary to abolish him.
stops.quote_source: God and the State (Dieu et l'Etat), ch. II, written 1871, published posthumously 1882; translation by Benjamin Tucker
suggested_refs: Dieu et l'Etat, Geneva 1882, edited by Cafiero and Reclus from the 1871 manuscript

stops.name: Petrograd, the Confession out of the archive
stops.date_confidence: attested for publication in 1921; the first research pass gave 1919, which is when the manuscript surfaced rather than when it was printed
stops.campa: The revolution opens the police archives of the empire, and in a file of the Third Section somebody finds a hundred manuscript pages in Bakunin's hand addressed to Nicholas I. Vyacheslav Polonsky publishes it in 1921, seventy years after it was written. The saint of the barricades is suddenly also a prisoner writing to a Tsar in the voice of a repentant son. Anarchists read it as tactics, Bolsheviks read it as capitulation, and the argument does not end. Robert C. Howes puts it into English in 1977.
stops.quote: A strong dictatorial power will be indispensable, but one which would concern itself solely with raising the standard of living and education of the peasant masses.
stops.quote_source: Confession to Tsar Nicholas I, 1851, translated by Robert C. Howes, excerpted on marxists.org
suggested_refs: Polonsky's 1921 Moscow edition of the Confession; Howes, Cornell University Press, 1977

stops.name: Moscow, Steklov's four volumes
stops.date_confidence: attested; the edition ran 1934-1935, correcting the 1934-1936 span given in the first research pass
stops.campa: Yuri Steklov, Marxist historian and the first editor of Izvestia, spends years assembling Bakunin's collected works and letters, and four volumes come out in Moscow between 1934 and 1935. Then the edition stops. Steklov is arrested in February 1938 in the Great Purge, and dies on the fifteenth of September 1941 in a Saratov prison, of dysentery and exhaustion, aged sixty-eight. The state that traced its descent through the winning side of the Hague quarrel prints no further volume of the loser for decades.
suggested_refs: Sobranie sochinenii i pisem, ed. Yu. M. Steklov, 4 vols., Moscow 1934-1935
sources: Soviet publishing history of the Bakunin edition

stops.name: Barcelona, the collectives
stops.date_confidence: attested for the July 1936 rising in Barcelona; the doctrinal descent from Bakunin is a historiographical reading, not a documented citation chain
stops.campa: The generals rise in July and the workers of Barcelona break them in the streets, and for some months the CNT and the FAI run the city, the factories, the trams, and a front in Aragon by committee. The anarchists who do it cite Bakunin by name against every proposal to build a state in order to win the war with one. It is the nearest thing to a practical afterlife his side of the Hague quarrel ever gets. Noam Chomsky will later call his forecast of the other road one of the few predictions in the social sciences that came true.
stops.quote: Freedom can be created only by freedom, by a total rebellion of the people, and by a voluntary organization of the people from the bottom up.
stops.quote_source: Statism and Anarchy, 1873, translation on marxists.org
suggested_refs: The CNT-FAI collectives of Barcelona and Aragon, 1936-1937
